Paid, Earned, Shared, Owned Media Explained

By lowob · 6 March 2026 · 4-minute read · Growth

Every channel falls into paid, earned, shared or owned media. Paid is bought, earned is given, shared is borrowed, owned is kept. A working system routes attention from the first three toward owned media, so companies should build the owned layer before rented channels become the whole plan.

Every channel a company could use to reach anyone falls into one of four kinds of media. The categories are old, but they remain the clearest way to see where control and cost actually sit.

The four

Paid media is attention you buy. Search and social ads, programmatic display and video, sponsored content, paid creator posts, affiliate commissions, clipping programs. You control the message and the timing; the platform or partner controls the access and the price. It starts when you pay and stops when you stop.

Earned media is attention other people give you without payment. Press coverage, reviews, organic mentions, word of mouth, unpaid creator content, podcast invitations. You control none of it directly, which is exactly why it carries trust. It is unpredictable, slow to build, and the cheapest form of credibility available once it arrives.

Shared media is attention that happens on social platforms and in communities, where you participate but do not own the space. Your accounts, your community channels, your presence in other people's groups. You control what you post; the platform controls who sees it and can change the rules on a Tuesday.

Owned media is attention on property you control. Your website, your email list, your content, your product's own messaging, your events. You control everything except whether anyone shows up, which is the whole challenge of it.

What each actually costs

Paid media costs money on a meter. Its price is set by how many other companies are bidding for the same attention, which is why it is expensive where the crowd is and cheap where it is not.

Earned media costs time, relationships, and having something worth saying. It also costs the discipline to accept that it cannot be scheduled.

Shared media costs staff time continuously and delivers reach that the platform can reduce at will. It is the category most companies overinvest in relative to what they control.

Owned media costs the most up front, building a list, producing content, maintaining a site, and the least over time, because nothing is rented.

How they fit together

A working system routes attention from the rented categories toward the owned one. Paid and shared media create the first contact. Earned media supplies the trust. Owned media is where the relationship is kept.

Concretely: a creator post (paid or earned) leads to a page you own, which asks for an email address, which lets you reach that person next year without paying the creator again. A press mention (earned) is republished on your newsroom page (owned) and shared on your accounts (shared). A programmatic buy (paid) drives to a guide (owned) that ranks for years.

Companies that skip the owned layer spend on paid and shared media forever, because they have nowhere to keep what they reach.

Why the categories matter more for restricted businesses

For a company in a category the ad platforms review, the paid and shared categories are partly closed: the largest ad platforms may refuse the account, and the social platforms may limit the reach of the content. That leaves the open band of paid media, affiliate, creator, clipping, programmatic, plus earned and owned.

That is not a weak position. It is a position that forces a company to build the two categories most businesses neglect, earned and owned, earlier than its competitors will.

Paid is bought, earned is given, shared is borrowed, owned is kept. Route attention from the first three toward the fourth, and build the owned layer before the rented ones become the whole plan.

lowob takeaways

  • Paid media starts when you pay and stops when you stop; its price is set by competing bidders.
  • Shared media is the category most companies overinvest in relative to what they control.
  • Restricted businesses are pushed to build earned and owned media earlier than competitors.
